Background and Summary The City of Wilton Manors (City) has been notified of significant rate increases by its wholesale water and large user wastewater treatment provider, the City of Fort Lauderdale (FLL). FLL’s September 1, 2026 letter identified wholesale water rate increases of 21.12% for FY 2027 and 23.25% for FY 2028. For wastewater, the large user rate approved for FY 2027 reflects an 18% increase; FLL has not yet provided information on wastewater rate adjustments beyond FY 2027. The City's 2025 Utility Rate Study (Rate Study) identified a wholesale/large user pass-through approach to handle the annual rate changes from FLL. However, these rate increases are significantly higher than the City anticipated. The City engaged Raftelis to review the financial impacts of these FLL rate adjustments and evaluate alternatives to implementation of the full pass-through. Based on our review, Raftelis supports FY 2027 rate adjustments of 10.9% for water and 8.1% for wastewater. Funding Transfer for Fire Prevention Services Outsourcing Transition - Approve the requested budget transfer from Fire Department Salaries and Benefits to Professional Services to support the transition of in-house fire prevention services to an outside professional service. The transition eliminates four full-time equivalent (FTE) positions, representing approximately $369,427 in annual salary and benefit expenditures. Transferring these savings to Professional Services allows the Department to fund a portion of the contracted prevention services while reducing long-term personnel costs and maintaining continuity of service. This approach provides greater operational flexibility, reduces administrative and staffing burdens, and allows the Department to align resources with current service delivery needs.

Without the addition of the drain-down piping, the filters are limited to slowly draining through the filter media, which would extend the necessary time that the system must be taken offline to prepare for backwash operation, and prevent the efficient operation of the system. Per direction in Requests for Information (RFI) 501 and 502, one run of four-inch and six-inch drain-down piping will be provided connecting from each pressure filter to the filter effluent-to-waste line, for a total of four runs. One six-inch electrically-actuated butterfly valve will be provided on each piping run. Electrical and instrumentation/control system improvements will be provided to accommodate the drain-down system addition. (d) Discussion: The City of Wilton Manors was awarded $1,000,000 through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for implementation of the Tidal Valve Program. The project is intended to improve the resiliency of the City’s stormwater system by reducing tidal backflow through existing stormwater outfalls during elevated tide conditions. The City issued Invitation to Bid (ITB) No. 2026-10 for the Tidal Valve Program on July 9, 2026, with bids opened on August 20, 2026. The project generally includes installation of inline backflow check valves at stormwater outfalls throughout the City, together with associated drainage structure modifications, pipe cleaning and repairs, pollution-retardant baffles, roadway and landscape restoration, and other related work. Following review of the bids, Southern Underground Industries, Inc. was determined to be the lowest responsive and responsible bidder. The final Schedule of Values establishes a construction amount of $1,354,231.30. Mr. Ennis reported that as part of the annual resurfacing program, the city evaluates the existing water, sewer, reclaimed and drainage facilities to ensure that no repairs are needed prior to the resurfacing of the roadway. As determined by pipe inspections, the existing drainage pipes within the following rights of way are in need of repair prior to resurfacing. Work Order No. 18 provides for the rehabilitation of approximately 2,200 linear feet of drainage pipes along Butler Street, Ferndale Avenue, Georgetown Avenue, Gulfview Drive, Leonard Weaver Boulevard, Stan Drive, Sherry Lane, and Veracruz Drive ranging in size between 15-inches to 48-inches, as further described in the exhibit provided. Cured-In-Place Pipe (CIPP) rehabilitation is a cost-effective and non-intrusive method of pipe repair. The CIPP restores the structural integrity of stormwater piping, reduces infiltration and eliminates leaking joints.

During the course of pre-inspection cleaning, the contractor encountered multiple runs of pipe which were of larger size than what was indicated in the city's existing records and for which the cleaning prices had been quoted. Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC): The BRIC provides grants to States and local governments to implement long-term hazard mitigation measures after a major disaster declaration. Projects aim to categorically shift the federal focus away from reactive disaster spending and toward research-supported, proactive investment in community resilience. Examples of BRIC projects are ones that demonstrate innovative approaches to partnerships, such as shared funding mechanisms, and/or project design. For example, an innovative project may bring multiple funding sources or in-kind resources from a range of private and public sector partners. Or an innovative project may offer multiple benefits to a community in addition to the benefit of risk reduction. Summary Explanation/Background Information on Agenda Request: The U.S. Department of Transportation, Federal Railroad Administration published a Notice of Funding Opportunity for a Crossing Safety Program to fund highway-rail or pathway-rail grade crossing improvement projects, including, but not limited to, grade crossing elimination projects, that focus on improving the safety and mobility of people and goods. The City Commission authorized the City of Stuart to seek grants through GrantWorks, Contract Number RFP 2025-300 approved Grant Writing and Grant Management Services in order to prepare and submit a grant application to the U.S. Department of Transportation (“USDOT”), FY 2025-2026 Railroad Crossing Elimination (“Crossing Safety”).

The Crossing Safety Program is intended to fund highway-rail or pathway-rail grade crossing improvement projects, including but not limited to elimination projects that improve the safety and mobility of people and goods. Such projects will improve American rail infrastructure to enhance rail safety, improve the health and safety of communities, eliminate highway-rail and pathway-rail grade crossings that are frequently blocked by trains, or reduce the impacts that freight movement and railroad operations may have on underserved communities. Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC): The BRIC provides grants to States and local governments to implement long-term hazard mitigation measures after a major disaster declaration. Projects aim to categorically shift the federal focus away from reactive disaster spending and toward research-supported, proactive investment in community resilience. Examples of BRIC projects are ones that demonstrate innovative approaches to partnerships, such as shared funding mechanisms, and/or project design. For example, an innovative project may bring multiple funding sources or in-kind resources from a range of private and public sector partners. Or an innovative project may offer multiple benefits to a community in addition to the benefit of risk reduction. outgoing_grants.title: Evans Park Renovation – Officially Awarded The City has received an official $1.5 million LWCF grant award for the Evans Park Renovation Project, which ranked 3rd statewide. Evans Park is one of Mount Dora's most popular waterfront destinations for residents and visitors. However, the park currently lacks basic amenities, including public restrooms and supporting infrastructure. These limitations impact everyday park use and require the City to rent equipment or secure sponsorships to provide temporary amenities during special events. The $3 million renovation project will address these longstanding needs through the addition of permanent restrooms, a new outdoor amphitheater, waterfront trail, picnic and gathering areas, and other park improvements. These improvements will enhance the everyday experience for residents while providing the infrastructure needed to better accommodate community events and reduce the City's reliance on temporary facilities.

The County’s partnership with NMC and FAMU Pharmacy provides uninsured and underinsured low-income residents with access to life-saving medication and education . FAMU Pharmacy provides services at NMC locations where patients can fill prescriptions and receive assistance with prescription costs through the Prescription Assistance Program (PAP). In FY 2026, FAMU Pharmacy filled nearly 4,400 prescriptions for NMC patients that reside in the Frenchtown, Griffin Heights, and Bond communities with a retail value of $ 936,807. The retail value of the prescriptions varies each year based on the type of prescriptions provided to patients. The Diabetes Collaborative Partnership Program provides diabetic patient s with information on the proper use of medications and instructions on how to manage blood pressure, cholesterol, and glucose. Many of the participants in the Diabetes Collaborative Partnership Program receive prescriptions through PAP. Funding provided to FAMU Pharmacy supports the costs for staffing positions for the Pharmaceutical Services and the Diabetes Collaborative Partnership Program.

He highlighted Chief Anderson's more than 15 years of service to Groveland, 23 years in law enforcement, bachelor's degree in criminal justice, and most recent role as Special Operations Lieutenant. Public Safety Director Carroll stated that all three internal candidates had performed exceptionally well during the interview process. He explained that he had interviewed 51 of the Police Department's 54 sworn and civilian employees to better understand the department's strengths, challenges, and personnel. He emphasized that Chief Anderson was responsible for leading every department member, regardless of their views on the selection process, and encouraged him to listen, seek guidance, support employees, and hold them accountable. Because of its remote location and high density of native vegetation, the donation parcel more than satisfies the off-site preserve requirements. The church has entered into an agreement with the Lake County School Board to grant the church-owned land to Eustis Elementary. The School Board's planned campus improvements, which include both this property and the main campus, will require demolishing or relocating the existing building that contains the thrift store. St. Thomas is requesting a Certificate of Appropriateness to construct a new building to house the thrift store. The applicant has provided anticipated floor plans and sketch elevations. This COA requests only the Historic Preservation Board's approval for the new thrift store construction, as the existing thrift store at 211 S Mary Street is outside the Washington Avenue Historic District.

N. Piggybacking The practice of procurement by one agency using the agreement of another agency is called piggybacking. The ability to piggyback onto an existing contract is not unlimited. The Subrecipient’s written procurement policy shall be submitted to the Division and shall allow for piggybacking. The existing contract shall contain language or other legal authority authorizing third parties to make purchases from the contract with the vendor’s consent. The terms and conditions of the new contract, including the Scope of Work, shall be substantially the same as those of the existing contract and approved by the Division. The piggyback contract shall not exceed the existing contract in scope or volume of goods or services. A Subrecipient shall not use the preexisting contract merely as a “basis to begin negotiations” for a broader or materially different contract. The contract was awarded to Medix Specialty Vehicles, LLC . Southwest Ambulance Sales, LLC is the authorized Medix dealer for the area, eligible to provide equipment under the contract. The County’s Purchasing Policy No. 96- 1, Section 6.06(E ) authorizes the County to purchase goods or services from authorized vendors listed on eligible contracts of cooperative purchasing organizations (a process known as “piggybacking” ). Such purchases may be made without conducting a separate competitive solicitation, provided the cooperative contract was awarded through full and open competition. Utilizing cooperative purchasing agreements allows the County to benefit from the combined purchasing power of multiple agencies, thereby reducing costs, administrative expenses, and procurement processing time. Background and Summary The City of Wilton Manors (City) has been notified of significant rate increases by its wholesale water and large user wastewater treatment provider, the City of Fort Lauderdale (FLL). FLL’s September 1, 2026 letter identified wholesale water rate increases of 21.12% for FY 2027 and 23.25% for FY 2028. For wastewater, the large user rate approved for FY 2027 reflects an 18% increase; FLL has not yet provided information on wastewater rate adjustments beyond FY 2027. The City's 2025 Utility Rate Study (Rate Study) identified a wholesale/large user pass-through approach to handle the annual rate changes from FLL. However, these rate increases are significantly higher than the City anticipated. The City engaged Raftelis to review the financial impacts of these FLL rate adjustments and evaluate alternatives to implementation of the full pass-through. Based on our review, Raftelis supports FY 2027 rate adjustments of 10.9% for water and 8.1% for wastewater. Public Works and Utilities Director Jennifer Spagnoli reported that during submittal coordination with the pressure filter vessel manufacturer, it was realized that four valved drain-down piping runs were not included in the original contract scope and should be added to facilitate the rapid draining of the filter vessels down to the top of media elevation to prepare for a backwash cycle. Without the addition of the drain-down piping, the filters are limited to slowly draining through the filter media, which would extend the necessary time that the system must be taken offline to prepare for backwash operation, and prevent the efficient operation of the system. Per direction in Requests for Information (RFI) 501 and 502, one run of four-inch and six-inch drain-down piping will be provided connecting from each pressure filter to the filter effluent-to-waste line, for a total of four runs. One six-inch electrically-actuated butterfly valve will be provided on each piping run. Electrical and instrumentation/control system improvements will be provided to accommodate the drain-down system addition. (d) Discussion: The City of Wilton Manors was awarded $1,000,000 through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for implementation of the Tidal Valve Program. The project is intended to improve the resiliency of the City’s stormwater system by reducing tidal backflow through existing stormwater outfalls during elevated tide conditions. The City issued Invitation to Bid (ITB) No. 2026-10 for the Tidal Valve Program on July 9, 2026, with bids opened on August 20, 2026. The project generally includes installation of inline backflow check valves at stormwater outfalls throughout the City, together with associated drainage structure modifications, pipe cleaning and repairs, pollution-retardant baffles, roadway and landscape restoration, and other related work. Following review of the bids, Southern Underground Industries, Inc. was determined to be the lowest responsive and responsible bidder. The final Schedule of Values establishes a construction amount of $1,354,231.30. Mr. Ennis reported that as part of the annual resurfacing program, the city evaluates the existing water, sewer, reclaimed and drainage facilities to ensure that no repairs are needed prior to the resurfacing of the roadway. As determined by pipe inspections, the existing drainage pipes within the following rights of way are in need of repair prior to resurfacing. Work Order No. 18 provides for the rehabilitation of approximately 2,200 linear feet of drainage pipes along Butler Street, Ferndale Avenue, Georgetown Avenue, Gulfview Drive, Leonard Weaver Boulevard, Stan Drive, Sherry Lane, and Veracruz Drive ranging in size between 15-inches to 48-inches, as further described in the exhibit provided. Cured-In-Place Pipe (CIPP) rehabilitation is a cost-effective and non-intrusive method of pipe repair. The CIPP restores the structural integrity of stormwater piping, reduces infiltration and eliminates leaking joints.

The NPCSS Program (also referred to as ‘the Program’) is built to strengthen the community by helping nonprofits offer the care and support people need after disaster, so residents can recover and prepare for the future. This RFA, the first in a series of funding opportunities under the NPCSS Program, is specifically focused on identifying subrecipients who will provide mental health and wraparound support services as described in this document. This is not a grantmaking opportunity where organizations apply to meet their individual needs; this is a solicitation where the City is procuring a specific set of services to meet the needs of city residents. Award CDBG-DR Funds for Mike Greenwell Regional Park Improvements Item Summary: Awards $50,000,000 in Community Development Block Grant – Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) funds for eligible design and construction costs associated with improvements to Mike Greenwell Regional Park. The proposed project includes replacement and renovation of agricultural and community facilities, site and accessibility improvements, and construction of a community and agricultural education center and covered outdoor educational and event platform. The improvements are intended to address documented Hurricane Ian impacts, restore community and agricultural functions, and improve the site’s resilience and emergency-support capacity. Board Discussion: County Staff presented the item to the Board. The Board discussed the timeline for the next 30 months regarding design and permitting for finalization of the most effective use of the $50 million based on feedback from the public and Board direction. There was continued Board discussions with Staff reminding the Board that the item is only a concept plan and that no architectural or engineering work has been done.
